[PAPER_0030, relevance_score=0.244] We assumed that the EEQ would have three expressions: EEP (people's belief that they have the right to experience positive emotions), EEN (people's belief that they have the right to experience negative emotions), and EEU (people's cognitive and emotional response toward others' failure to meet their emotional needs). We predicted that items from our three dimensions would emerge as distinct factors. We also expected a positive relationship between the three dimensions as they all represent the concept of emotional entitlement.

[PAPER_0038, relevance_score=0.275] Data Analyses

Study 1 focused on exploring the factor structure of the EEQ. Rather than relying on the chi-squared test which is sensitive to sample size (Marsh et al., 2005), commonly applied goodness-of-fit indices were examined with their respective thresholds (Hu & Bentler, 1999): namely, the Tucker-Lewis index (TLI; ≥.95 for good, ≥.90 for acceptable) and the root-mean-square error of approximation (RMSEA; ≤.06 for good, ≤.08 for acceptable) with its 90% confidence interval (CI).

items.paper_content_quotes:
[PAPER_0029, relevance_score=0.363] Study 1-Scale Construction and Exploratory Factor Analysis

The first study was designed to create a scale that captures our proposed theoretical definition of emotional entitlement. We administered items related to the experience of emotional entitlement using an online survey platform. Participants were asked to answer a battery of items related to their perception of their right to feel positive emotions, their right to feel negative emotions, and their uncompromised emotional expectations. Following data collection, we performed an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) on these items.

[PAPER_0033, relevance_score=0.509] Participants and Procedure

Upon receiving approval from Peres academic center's institutional review board, written informed consent was obtained from all of the participants included in the study. In Study 1, 200 participants (69.1% female) from Israel were recruited through convenience sampling by research assistants who contacted the participants through social networks. The participants volunteered to complete the study's questionnaires, which were provided via an electronic link.
